name: Supporting First Generation Families
title: Supporting First Generation Families
answer: Supporting first generation families means giving students whose parents did not attend college extra help with applications, financial aid, and campus life, because their families may not know how these systems work. The book argues this targeted support is worth the investment, while warning schools to think carefully about which kinds of family support actually change outcomes.

sections.body: First generation students face hurdles that other students do not, since their families may be unfamiliar with how college applications, financial aid, and campus life operate. The idea is to direct support at these students and their families rather than assuming the standard information channels reach everyone. The book treats this as a worthwhile investment, but it also cautions that not every form of family involvement produces results. The problem it solves is the gap in knowledge and confidence that can keep first generation students from completing the steps to enrollment. It also pushes schools to test their assumptions about what families need instead of adding outreach by habit.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, schools can run family nights, provide translated guides, and hold personal conversations so first generation families understand each step of the process. Messages can be carried in families' own languages through TalkingPoints, as described elsewhere in the book, and BigFuture offers information families can explore together. The goal is for families to feel confident supporting their children rather than overwhelmed by the process. The book does not divide these practices by grade band, so the same mix of translated materials, personal contact, and shared exploration applies across the secondary years. The emphasis stays on helping families understand the process, not on flooding them with more information.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book reports that a chatbot trial found first generation students gained the most from outreach during the summer (Nurshatayeva et al., 2021). It also reports that adding parents to text messages did not increase the effect in one trial (Castleman & Page, 2017), where text outreach raised on time enrollment by about 3 points but messages to parents added nothing beyond messages to students. The book reads this not as proof that families do not matter, but as a reason for schools to think carefully about what kind of family support actually helps. These findings carry the book's own citations and figures as stated.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are about not overreading the evidence. A null result for parent text messages does not mean families are unimportant, and the book explicitly warns against that conclusion. Schools still have to decide which family supports to use, how to translate and deliver them, and how to hold personal conversations without overwhelming families. Those choices stay with the people running the program, not with any tool or message template. The aim is family confidence, and the book treats that as a judgment schools must make rather than something a messaging system can settle on its own.
